Hi! I am a 6th grader from Vietnam who loves coding and game design. My team is building a game/software application to help farmers use NASA data for the 'Field Shift' challenge.

You should join my team if you love using technology to solve real-world problems. I am looking for teammates who have skills in:

Coding / Game Development.

Researching NASA Earth observation data.

Pitching and presentation. Let's build an awesome app together!
summary:
Chronicles of Cosmic Relics is an interactive educational 2D adventure and puzzle mobile game for Android and iOS designed to introduce students and the public to NASA’s legacy spacecraft. Players take on the role of a futuristic Digital Heritage Recovery Robot exploring the Moon and Mars using real-world coordinates.
To address the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge, our game transforms historical space exploration into hands-on storytelling. By integrating NASA’s open datasets—including 3D Resources, AppEEARS elevation heightmaps, and Solar System Exploration mission logs—players navigate authentic lunar and Martian terrains. Upon locating iconic relics like the Apollo landers, Surveyor probes, or the Opportunity rover, players complete tactile mini-games such as wiping dust off solar panels, aligning antennas, and repairing circuits.
Each restored spacecraft illuminates on a global digital heritage map, unlocking historical facts and emotional dialogues. This project is important because it turns passive history into active, empathetic learning, inspiring the next generation to remember the robotic pioneers that paved the way for human spaceflight.
details:
What it does and how it works
Chronicles of Cosmic Relics is a free educational game about the equipment NASA left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. The player is a Heritage Recovery Robot from the future whose mission is to find these silent machines and bring their stories back.

The game includes 21 relics: 9 on the Moon (Ranger 7, Surveyor 1, 3 and 7, Apollo 11, 14, 15, 17 and LCROSS), 8 on Mars (Viking 1 and 2, Pathfinder/Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight and Ingenuity) and 4 in deep space (Pioneer 10 and 11, Voyager 1 and 2). Each relic sits at its real landing coordinates on a latitude–longitude map; the deep-space map is a star chart showing each probe's real direction of travel.

To restore a relic, the player:

  1. drives the robot across the map, following a signal arrow that shows the real distance to the nearest relic;
  2. scans it to open its mission file (real coordinates, landing date, final status, science highlights);
  3. plays a mini-game: wiping dust off solar panels, turning an antenna back toward Earth, or repairing a logic circuit;
  4. answers a quiz question to "restore its memory," with a short science explanation;
  5. lights it up as a golden beacon on the Heritage Map.

Spacecraft that are still working, such as Curiosity and New Horizons, also appear on the maps but do not need rescuing, so players learn the difference between active and retired missions.

Benefits and intended impact
Most students know Apollo 11, but few know how many machines are still out there or what each one taught us. The game turns that history into exploration: students learn by locating, repairing and questioning, not by reading a list. It is bilingual (Vietnamese and English), runs in any browser on phones, tablets and computers with no installation, and works offline after the first visit, which matters for schools with weak internet. It collects no personal data. Our goal is that every player leaves with one idea: these machines were abandoned, but they should never be forgotten.

Tools and technologies
HTML5, CSS and plain JavaScript, with no external libraries. Canvas 2D draws the maps and animations, and Web Audio plays the sound. The game is published as a Progressive Web App on GitHub Pages and as an Android APK (packaged with Apktool, signed with uber-apk-signer). A Python build script reproduces every version. Fonts are Be Vietnam Pro and Chakra Petch (SIL Open Font License). All mission data comes from public NASA sources (NSSDCA, NASA Science, LROC, Apollo Lunar Surface Journal). No challenge dataset was used and no AI/ML model runs in or was trained for the game. SI tools used during development are declared in the SI section and in our README.

Creativity
Instead of a museum-style list, each relic becomes a character with its own voice and story. Viking 1, which lost contact in 1982 after a mistaken command turned its antenna away from Earth, is restored by aiming its antenna back home. Spirit's dusty panels are wiped clean by hand. The Heritage Map slowly fills with golden lights, turning a history lesson into a personal act of remembrance.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific accuracy: every relic lists its NASA sources, and we mark where we tell a story rather than state a fact. For example, Opportunity's famous "My battery is low and it's getting dark" is a journalist's paraphrase, and the game says so.
  • Honesty about limits: the terrain is illustrative (only features and relics are at real coordinates), and deep-space distances are 2026 estimates.
  • Accessibility: simple touch controls, mouse and keyboard support, bilingual text, offline play.
  • Privacy and safety: no accounts, no data collection, and no names, voices or images of team members under 18.
